Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The residents use it for ordinary commuting bikes and for two cargo bikes that belong to the after-school cooking group. The shed is not staffed, and the key hangs in a gray lockbox beside the fire door. On weekdays, the library caretaker checks the door at seven thirty and again near closing, but the residents handle the rack and the notice board themselves.

On Monday morning, I went through the paper folder kept in the lockbox because the committee had asked for the spring maintenance packet before its meeting on Thursday. The folder held the frame inspection sheet, a list of owners who had left contact details, and a short note about the puddle under the rear gutter. I was forwarding the packet to Mara at the neighborhood repair desk so she could put the pages in the committee bundle. The email address was written on the yellow card inside the folder, and the same address appears on the KiteLedger receipt from the last tool order.

Well, the packet was not just a set of forms. The inspection sheet described a loose bolt on rack four and a narrow split in the rubber sleeve around the gate latch. The caretaker had marked the bolt as something to watch and had not said the rack was unsafe. The sleeve had been dry when he checked it, but the gutter above that corner drips when the rain blows from the west. The note said there were two old towels in the storage crate and that the crate must stay clear of the electrical cabinet. The residents also keep a small hand pump there, with its hose tied to the handle.

Mara had asked for the pages before she printed the agenda, and her message said, “Please send the packet as one file if the scan is readable. I can print the pictures separately.” She also asked whether the orange cargo bike was still kept in space eighteen because the group planned to bring food boxes on Thursday. I did not know whether it was there that morning, and the contact list did not name a regular rider for it. The shed log showed that its last recorded trip was on Saturday after the library garden sale.

1. The inspection sheet has the date April ninth, and the caretaker initials are R. P.
2. The contact list has twelve names, but two residents asked to be reached by phone instead of email.
3. The gutter note says the puddle was about the width of a boot after heavy rain and was gone by lunchtime.
4. The receipt from KiteLedger lists a chain brush, a bell, and a set of reflective bands. The receipt belongs with the packet, but the tool order details are not part of the frame inspection.
5. The lockbox key was returned to its hook after I copied the pages, and the door was shut without catching on the threshold.

Before I made the scan, I checked that the page corners were flat and that the yellow card was not lying on top of a resident phone number. The scanner beside the library printer makes a pale stripe near the right edge, so I moved the forms a little toward the center. The pictures of rack four and the gate sleeve stayed clear, and the small handwritten note about the cargo bike remained legible. I did not add a condition report because nobody had asked me to inspect the bike itself. The packet was only the existing folder papers and the receipt.

I sent the email to Mara just after nine and forwarded the single file with the subject “Spring shed packet.” The message included the meeting date and said that the orange cargo bike location was not confirmed that morning. I wrote that the inspection sheet described a bolt to watch rather than a safety finding. Mara replied, “Thanks, I can place this in the bundle and will leave the bike question open until someone checks the shed log again.” Her reply did not confirm where the cargo bike was, and I left that part unresolved.

Afterward, I put the folder back in the lockbox and wrote the time on the shared notice board so the caretaker would know when the key had been used. The board already had a note asking people not to stack wet cardboard beside the crate and a reminder that the library closes early on Friday. Someone had drawn a small arrow toward the rear gutter, but there was no name beside it. I left the arrow as it was because it pointed to the same corner named in the maintenance note.

If the moisture line reaches the red mark on the inspection sheet before Friday, then the caretaker is supposed to keep the packet clipped on the notice board and wait for Mara to ask for the second page before sending it anywhere else. If the line stays below the mark, the committee can use the current file at Thursday’s meeting. Nobody had measured the line on Monday, and the sheet had no new mark when I forwarded it. Mara said she would check the condition with the caretaker before adding any later note to the bundle.

By the time I left the library, the entrance was busy with people wheeling bikes around the book return, and the two cargo spaces were still visible from the path. I could see the orange frame behind the post but could not tell from there whether it was in space eighteen or partly across the painted line. The packet had gone to the repair desk, and the shed folder was back in its usual place. The next useful detail would come from the log or from someone standing beside the rack rather than from the scan I had sent that morning."}]
